title: Teo Marchetti

pages.text:
The bell above the bakery door didn’t ring. It clattered, a dull, heavy sound that matched the grey morning. Juno pushed through the door, her yellow raincoat squeaking against the wet concrete floor. The smell hit her next: yeast, warm butter, and the sharp tang of burnt sugar. It was the best smell in the world, and it made her stomach growl loud enough to echo off the tiled walls.

A boy stood behind the counter, hunched over a bicycle wheel. He was tall for twelve, with messy black hair sticking out from under a green cap and round glasses sliding down his nose. A canvas tool belt hung loosely at his waist, filled with wrenches that jingled softly. He didn’t look up.

"Closed," he said, his voice flat. "We open at eight. It is seven-thirty."

Juno looked at the clock on the wall. It was seven-thirty.

"I need help," Juno said. "Big help. The kind that involves saving the world, or at least the harbor. And I’m out of money, but I have a very loyal crab."

The boy finally looked up. His eyes were dark and tired, framed by smudges of grease. "I don’t help people who talk to crabs," he said. "Unless it’s a joke. Is it a joke?"

Juno looked down at the blue teapot shell nestled in her raincoat pocket. Barnacle was silent, but she could feel his irritation vibrating against her hip.

"No," Juno said. "It’s not a joke. And I’m not asking for a loan. I’m asking for a mechanic."

The boy sighed, a long, deflating sound. He picked up a rag and began wiping his hands. "You have five minutes to explain why I shouldn’t throw you out. And then I’m making a croissant for myself, so don’t block the oven."
pages.image: Juno in a yellow raincoat standing in a bakery, facing a boy with round glasses and a green cap who is hunched over a bicycle wheel, warm interior lighting.

pages.text:
Barnacle was not a subtle creature. He was, in fact, the opposite of subtle. He was a hermit crab the size of a thumb, living in a chipped blue teapot that looked like it had been left in a dishwasher for a century. He was currently sitting on the counter, tapping one claw against a glass jar of blueberries.

Tap. Tap. Tap.

"Is that a bug?" Teo asked, staring at the shell.

"No," Juno said, trying to keep her voice steady. "That is Barnacle. He is my advisor. And he is very angry because you are blocking his view of the jam."

Teo adjusted his glasses. "He’s a crab. Crabs don’t have views. They have legs. And that shell is chipped. It looks like it fell off a shelf."

Barnacle let out a noise that sounded like a tiny, angry hiccup. "Honestly!" he snapped. "I have survived three shipwrecks and a very rude seagull, and now I have to deal with a grease monkey who can’t even appreciate a vintage teapot."

Teo blinked. He looked at Juno. Then he looked at the crab. "I didn’t hear anything," Teo said. "Did he... did he move?"

"He spoke," Juno said. "He insulted your shoes. They’re ugly."

"My shoes are vintage work boots," Teo said, offended. "And I didn’t hear a thing. You’re either very young or very lost. There is a difference, though I can’t tell which one you are right now."

Juno took a deep breath. She was going to lose this. She could feel it. Her secret fear, the one that lived under her ribs, was starting to poke its head out. *You are just loud. You are just a girl talking to herself in a bakery.*

"Okay," Juno said. "Proof. Barnacle, spell it out."

"Spell what?" Barnacle asked, crossing his tiny arms. "I am not a parrot. I am a dignified crustacean."

"Spell his fear," Juno whispered. "The one he thinks no one knows."

Barnacle looked at Teo. A slow, smug grin spread across his face. "Oh, he’s got a fear, does he? Good. Let’s see how brave he is now."
pages.image: A small hermit crab in a blue teapot shell sitting on a bakery counter, looking smug, with a boy in a green cap looking confused in the background.

pages.text:
Teo crossed his arms. "This is getting ridiculous. I have customers coming in. I have a reputation to maintain. I am not going to listen to a girl and a bug play charades."

Barnacle picked up a small, smooth pebble from the counter. There were three others sitting in a row, like dominoes. He nudged the first one with his claw. It rolled to the side.

"W," Barnacle said.

"Water," Teo said, his voice dropping an octave. "Why is he saying water?"

Barnacle nudged the second pebble. "T."

"T?" Juno prompted. "Keep going, Barnacle."

"E," Barnacle said.

Teo’s face had gone pale. He stared at the pebbles. W. T. E.

"Deep water," Juno said softly. "He can’t swim well. He’s terrified of it. He thinks if he goes in, he’ll sink and never come back. And he’s never told anyone. Not his mom. Not his friends. Not me."

Teo didn’t move. He didn’t breathe. The bakery was silent, except for the hum of the refrigerator and the ticking of the clock.

"How..." Teo started. His voice cracked. "How did he know that?"

"He listens," Juno said. "The sea listens. And Barnacle listens for the sea. He heard you, Teo. He heard you practicing your breathing exercises in the bakery at night, pretending you were counting croissants. He heard you shaking."

Teo looked at his hands. They were trembling. He had always kept it secret. He was the fixer. He was the one who understood gears and engines. He was not the boy who cried in the bathroom when the shower got too loud.

"He’s a crab," Teo whispered.

"He’s a friend," Juno corrected. "And he knows things. He knows that the tide is broken. He knows that if we don’t fix it, the sea will forget this bay forever. And he’s offering you a job. You’re the best mechanic in town. I need you."

Teo looked at the pebbles. Then he looked at Barnacle, who was currently grooming his whiskers with an air of supreme satisfaction.

"If you are lying," Teo said, "I will make you a sandwich made of old bread and despair."

"I accept the challenge," Barnacle said. "But I prefer my sandwiches with extra cheese."
pages.image: Teo standing still with pale face, looking at a row of pebbles on a counter, while a small crab in a teapot shell looks smug nearby.

pages.text:
Teo was quiet for a long time. The rain tapped against the window, a steady rhythm that usually helped him think. Today, it just made the world feel smaller. He picked up his wrench, then set it down. He picked it up again.

"Nine days," he said. "That’s what you said. Nine days until it’s too late."

"Grand Low," Juno clarified. "The night of the full moon. If the Clock doesn’t wind, the tide stops. Forever."

Teo shook his head. "It’s a clock. It’s brass. It’s a machine. Machines break, but they don’t stop breathing. Breathing is for people. And crabs."

"Exactly," Juno said. "And crabs are dying because the mud is drying up. Barnacle’s shell is cracking. I can see it. It’s not just about the boats, Teo. It’s about the life. The salt. The rhythm. If it stops, everything dies. The fish, the gulls, the mud, the... the feeling of the town."

Teo looked out the window. The street was grey and wet. The bakery was warm and safe, but it felt like a bubble. He could stay here. He could fix the bicycle, eat his croissant, and pretend the world wasn’t ending. Or he could go out into the mud and try to save a sea that he was terrified of.

The thought made his stomach turn. But then he looked at Barnacle. The little crab was watching him with a kind of stubborn respect. It wasn’t pity. It was expectation.

"I don’t believe you," Teo said. "But I’m coming. If you’re wrong, I’m suing you for emotional damages."

"You won’t be able to afford the lawyer," Barnacle said. "I checked. You have four dollars and a half in your pocket."

"Shut up, Barnacle," Teo said, but he was smiling. It was a small, crooked smile, but it was there. He pulled a wrench from his belt and tucked it into his pocket. "I need to pack. And Juno? If this is a dream, I’m going to be very angry."

"It’s not a dream," Juno said. "It’s worse. It’s real."

Teo nodded. He grabbed his green cap from the hook by the door. "Meet me at the lighthouse. In an hour. Bring your crab. And Juno?"

"Yes?"

"Bring a flashlight. I hate the dark."
pages.image: Teo smiling slightly, holding a wrench, while Juno in a yellow raincoat looks hopeful, with a small crab in a teapot shell on the counter between them.

pages.text:
They walked out into the rain. The air was cold and smelled of wet stone and brine. Teo walked fast, his boots splashing through the puddles. Juno followed, her heart pounding. For the first time since she had arrived, she didn’t feel like a suitcase nobody unpacked. She felt like a captain with a crew.

Behind them, the bakery door swung shut. Through the glass, they could see the boy’s reflection in the window, distorted and small. Then he was gone.

Juno stopped at the corner of the harbor road. The mud was thick and grey, stretching out to the low-tide line. The boats lay tilted in the silt, their masts pointing accusingly at the sky.

"So," Juno said. "What do we do first?"

Barnacle, who had been riding in her pocket, climbed out and sat on the wet pavement. He looked out at the harbor, his eyes bright and hard.

"We go to the Lighthouse," he said. "But we do not go alone. There are others. Creatures. Old ones. They remember the Keeper. They will not like you, girl. You are too loud. You are too bright. You smell like bread and fear."

"I do not smell like fear," Juno said.

"You smell like salt," Barnacle said. "And that is dangerous. The sea is angry, Juno. It has been waiting for a year. It is not going to forgive you easily. So listen. And for the love of all that is salty, do not let it hear you think."

Juno looked at Teo. He was staring at the water, his jaw tight. He was scared. But he was here.

"We’re going to the lighthouse," Juno said. "Right now."

"Beg your pardon?" Barnacle said, adjusting his teapot. "I said listen. Not run. The sea does not answer the loud. It answers the listening."

Juno took a deep breath. She let the rain hit her face. She let the cold seep into her bones. And then, she started to walk.
pages.image: Juno and Teo walking on a muddy path toward a distant lighthouse, with a small crab in a teapot shell sitting on the pavement in the foreground, rainy grey atmosphere.

summary: Juno meets Teo Marchetti at the bakery and convinces him to join her quest to save the tide by using Barnacle to spell out Teo's secret fear of deep water. Teo reluctantly agrees to help, revealing his mechanical skills and his fear of the dark, and the group sets out toward the lighthouse. Barnacle warns Juno that the sea is angry and that she must learn to listen rather than just speak.
